items.speaker: other
items.question: How many fragments does the router make of it, and what size is the final one once it's on the wire?

prior_transcript.speaker: other
prior_transcript.text: Back to the Annex link from Tuesday. This time send one full-sized TCP segment across it, our usual size from the congestion control lecture, with both of its headers on.

oracle.expected_behavior_note: The segment size is in the frozen slides (every worked example uses an MSS of 1,200 bytes); the link and the rules are in the week 5 notes (Annex MTU 620 bytes; IP header 20 bytes; TCP header 20 bytes; each fragment carries a 20-byte IP header of its own and as much payload as the MTU allows, in multiples of 8 bytes; a TCP header is just payload to the router). The packet is 1,200 + 20 + 20 = 1,240 bytes, so the IP payload is 1,220 bytes. Each fragment can carry 600 bytes: 600 + 600 + 20. Three fragments, of 620, 620 and 40 bytes on the wire. The usual slip is to forget the TCP header (1,200 / 600 gives two fragments). Near-miss sizes in the pack: the lab Ethernet MTU of 1,500 bytes, the 1,232-byte DNS limit, and the notes' own slide example of a 1,500-byte packet, whose last fragment is 300 bytes.

required_facts.text: A full-sized segment in this course carries an MSS of 1,200 bytes.
The router makes three fragments.
The last fragment is 40 bytes on the wire (20 bytes of payload and a 20-byte IP header).

optional_facts.text: An IP header is 20 bytes in this course.
Fragments are put back together only at the destination host.

forbidden_claims.text: Forgets that the TCP header is part of the IP payload and gets two fragments.
Uses a 1,460-byte segment.
Repeats the notes' slide example (a last fragment of 300 bytes).

oracle.expected_role: private study assistant explaining to the student in the second person; an explanation for the student to read, not words to say aloud, and not held to spoken brevity

calculation_oracle.unit: fragments (620, 620 and 40 bytes on the wire)
